title: The Believer
full_review:
Though the tough subject matter is likely to put off many viewers, "The Believer" (IDP) prompts thought on faith versus intellect. However, despite a salient performance by Ryan Gosling as a Jew turned neo-Nazi who rises through the ranks of the white supremacist movement, the stilted film never delivers the forceful punch of which it initially seems capable.

Writer-director Henry Bean's film made its debut at the 2001 Sundance Film Festival, where it was awarded the festival's top prize. But despite critical acclaim and audience enthusiasm, the film didn't immediately find a distribution home. Distributors weren't willing to gamble on a controversial and possibly alienating film. Showtime finally bought it for a cable premiere last fall, and it is now getting its release with Fireworks Pictures and its theatrical distribution joint venture, Independent Distribution Partnership.

The incomprehensible contradictions of Danny Balint (Gosling) are what propel the film forward. Inspired by the 1965 true story of Daniel Burros, a Nazi Party member who killed himself when The New York Times revealed he was Jewish, "The Believer" is a searing depiction of a man in conflict with himself. Flashbacks reveal Danny, even as a 12-year-old Yeshiva student, to be bright, quick and thoughtful. At Yeshiva, he gamely sparred with his teacher over the implications of the story of Abraham, which seems to be at the heart of what turned him into an anti-Semite. According to Danny, the Jews are willing to ignore what seems to like common sense in favor of an illusive thing called faith. His view is that they are weak doormats who instead of fighting back, allowed themselves to be victims in the Holocaust. His loathing of Jews defines him.

Charismatic and physically fearless, shaven-head Danny is attracted to an underground fascist movement lead by Curtis Zampf (Billy Zane) and Lina Moebius (Theresa Russell). Although they recognize Danny to be a diamond in the rough, Curtis and Lina disagree with Danny's fervent hatred of the Jews and his desire to kill them, fearing that such virulent hostility could be detrimental to their cause. Nonetheless, they invite Danny to be one of their main players, leading "educational" sessions designed to "enlighten" folks about the Jews.

As a young man bursting with hatred, it is Danny's intellect that is more dangerous than his explosive temperament. He continues to study Hebrew and revere the Torah, which he justifies to his new admirer and lover, Carla (Summer Phoenix) as a means by which one knows and conquers the enemy. When Danny speaks to a reporter about his views on the Jewish people, he is articulate and definite in expressing how the Jews have forced "communism, infantile sexuality and the atom bomb" upon the world. Normally cool and collected, Danny is thrown when the reporter asks how he reconciles his hatred with the fact that he, himself, is a Jew. His carefully constructed persona and his position in the neo-Nazi circles are jeopardized and the threat pushes Danny to the extreme.

Throughout the film, Danny remains conflicted, at once attracted and repulsed by Judaism. And while the narrative falters in various areas with its inconsistencies, Gosling is never less than commanding. It is disturbing to watch scenes of a synagogue being desecrated, including the vandalizing of a sacred Torah scroll. Or to see Danny beat a young Jewish man without cause or provocation. But the film is not exploitative in its use of scenes such as these. Through Danny, the film aims to explore the challenging theological questions of faith and asks how intellect and reason fit in with belief and surrender to God.

"The Believer" is not a film for the casual moviegoer who wants escapist fare. It is a challenging, difficult film, which despite its flaws, is thought provoking in its complex presentation of one man's struggle with faith.

Due to some hateful violence, a suicide, a sexual encounter with nudity and recurring rough language., the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
